tulpaObs

false zeros from imperfect detection

tulpaObs fits Bayesian models for species surveys with imperfect detection, such as site occupancy from repeated visits, N-mixture abundance from replicated counts, distance and removal sampling, and vegetation cover.

A site can read zero because the species is absent, or because it was present and missed on every visit. Each model writes the ecological state (occupied or not, how many individuals) and the detection process as separate levels and integrates the latent state out of the likelihood, so occupancy and detection come back as separate estimates. Each model supplies its observation likelihood to the tulpa engine, which fits it by Laplace approximation, by nested Laplace integration over the hyperparameters, or by the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS). You choose the model through a family object, write spatial, temporal and random effects inside the formula, and pick the inference method for each fit.

tulpaObs supports:

  • Occupancy, abundance and cover models. Single-season, dynamic, integrated, false-positive, time-to-detection and community occupancy; N-mixture, distance, removal and double-observer abundance; and a hurdle model for vegetation cover. One fitter, tobs(), takes a family constructor per model (families in the reference).
  • Structured effects inside the formula. Areal and continuous spatial fields, temporal processes and lme4-style random effects enter the occupancy or the detection formula as terms.
  • Several inference routes. Laplace approximation is the default; nested Laplace handles areal fields, NUTS gives the full posterior, and a Polya-Gamma Gibbs sampler is available for single-season and community models.
  • Simulation with known truth. Every family has a simulator that returns the data with the parameters that generated them, so a model can be checked against known values before it meets field data.

The package’s recovery tests are built on these simulators. Occupancy: tulpaObs vs INLA aggregated-binomial and Cover hurdle: tulpaObs vs INLA on simulated cover data compare fits with INLA on simulated data with known truth.

Installation

tulpaObs compiles C++17 code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools matching your R version
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install tulpaObs:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/tulpaObs")

pak installs tulpa and tulpaMesh from CRAN along with it. The build links against the BLAS and LAPACK libraries that R itself uses, so no other system library is needed. Tagged releases are listed on the releases page.

Optional: multithreading

OpenMP lets the community NUTS samplers (ms_occu(), ms_count(), jsdm(), ms_abun(), ms_dyn_occu()) evaluate their gradient on several CPU threads, set through n.threads.grad in the control list of tobs(). The per-species reduction runs in a fixed order, so the gradient is the same at any thread count.

Rtools on Windows and the default compiler on Linux include OpenMP. Without it, the package installs and runs on one thread.

macOS setup

Apple’s compiler needs an additional OpenMP runtime. Install it in Terminal:

brew install libomp

Before installing tulpaObs, add the settings for your Mac to ~/.R/Makevars, R’s personal compiler-settings file. Create the directory and file if needed.

Apple Silicon:

CPPFLAGS += -I/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/lib -lomp

Intel:

CPPFLAGS += -I/usr/local/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/usr/local/opt/libomp/lib -lomp

Usage

  1. Fit a model with tobs(): the occupancy formula, the data, a family such as occu(), the detection formula and the detection histories.
  2. Read the estimates with coef() or summary().
  3. Predict with predict() and check the fit with check_model().

peatland_occu is a synthetic survey shipped with the package: 120 sites visited four times, with elevation and wetness per site and survey effort per visit.

library(tulpaObs)

occ <- peatland_occu
fit <- tobs(
  ~ elevation + wetness,
  data = occ$occ.covs,
  family = occu(),
  detection = ~ effort,
  y = occ$y,
  visits = occ$det.covs
)
coef(fit)
#> psi_(Intercept)   psi_elevation     psi_wetness   p_(Intercept)  p_visit_effort 
#>     0.242198812    -0.505199672     0.691204862    -0.001590117     0.853642172

The psi_ coefficients belong to the occupancy formula and the p_ coefficients to the detection formula, both on the logit scale.

The detection histories y are a matrix with one row per site and one column per visit (1 detected, 0 not detected, NA missing). Site covariates are a data frame with one row per site, and covariates that change between visits are matrices of the same shape as y, passed through visits. tobs_format() and tobs_data() build the same input from matrices or from a long table with one row per site-visit; Shaping data for tobs() covers both.

Structured effects

Spatial fields, temporal processes and random effects are terms in the formula, and each enters the process whose formula it is written in:

~ elevation +
  spatial(graph = adj) +
  temporal(year, type = "ar1") +
  (1 | observer)

spatial() takes an adjacency matrix for areal models (ICAR by default, BYM2, CAR) or coordinates for continuous fields (model = "spde" or "gp"). Random effects follow lme4’s bar syntax, including correlated slopes, crossed and nested grouping. ?tobs_terms documents every term. Areal spatial occupancy with ICAR, BYM2, and CAR, Occupancy with a continuous SPDE spatial field and Random effects with lme4 bar syntax work through each.

Inference methods

method in tobs() selects the route: "laplace" (the default), "nested_laplace" for areal fields and the joint cover hurdle, "nuts" for the full posterior with split-Rhat and effective sample sizes, and "pg_gibbs", an exact Polya-Gamma Gibbs sampler, on single-season occupancy, t_occu() and the community families. An unsupported combination of family and method stops with the methods that family accepts.

Variance components of binary random effects are biased under the Laplace approximation when groups are small. An adaptive Gauss-Hermite pass corrects them by default; with eight observations per group it lowers the measured bias in the random-effect standard deviation from about 18 % to about 4 %, matching a NUTS fit (Random effects with lme4 bar syntax).

Checking and comparing fits

check_model() collects the sampler diagnostics, WAIC, a posterior predictive check, a zero-inflation test and Moran’s I in one report. waic() and loo() are the generics of the loo package, so loo::loo_compare() compares tulpaObs fits directly. Diagnostics: checking, comparing, and residuals covers the full workflow.

Documentation

Start with Getting started with tulpaObs: one path from simulated detection histories to a fitted, compared and predicted occupancy model.

  • Shaping data for tobs(): detection histories and covariates from matrices or long tables.
  • Single-season occupancy: the base model end to end, including when occupancy and detection cannot be separated.
  • Dynamic (multi-season) occupancy: colonisation and extinction across seasons.
  • Integrated occupancy: combining data sources: several detection processes sharing one occupancy state.
  • N-mixture abundance with tulpaObs: abundance from replicated counts.
  • Community models in tulpaObs: many species with shared community priors.
  • Cover hurdle (independent arms) and Cover hurdle on resurvey panels (MOTIVATE reduction): vegetation cover with zeros.
  • Areal spatial occupancy with ICAR, BYM2, and CAR and Occupancy with a continuous SPDE spatial field: spatial fields.
  • Random effects with lme4 bar syntax: grouped effects and the small-group correction.
  • Diagnostics: checking, comparing, and residuals: checking and comparing fits.
  • Occupancy: tulpaObs vs INLA aggregated-binomial and Cover hurdle: tulpaObs vs INLA on simulated cover data: comparisons with INLA.
  • Full reference: every function, grouped by job.

Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the GitHub issues. A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with reprex.
